article.title: Beyond Propensity Scores: Who Should Actually Receive the Campaign?
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: A propensity model estimates who is likely to convert, but the customers with the highest predicted conversion probability are not always the customers who should receive a campaign. Targeting is a decision problem, not only a prediction problem. Consider four conceptual customer types. Sure things are likely to buy whether or not they receive the treatment. Persuadables are more likely to buy because of the treatment. Lost causes are unlikely to buy either way. Some customers may even react negatively to contact. A standard propensity model can rank sure things very highly because their observed conversion rate is high. Sending them an expensive incentive may generate many conversions that would have happened anyway. Incremental targeting instead asks how treatment changes the outcome relative to no treatment. This is the idea behind uplift modeling and heterogeneous treatment effects. The decision rule should also include economics. Suppose a campaign creates an estimated one-percentage-point incremental conversion effect for a customer, and an incremental conversion is worth 3,000 yen in contribution margin. The expected incremental value is about 30 yen before treatment cost. If the contact and incentive cost 100 yen, the action is unattractive even though the treatment effect is positive. Uncertainty matters too. Individual treatment-effect estimates are noisy, especially when historical experiments are small or treatment assignment was not randomized. Teams should validate uplift by groups or score bands rather than treating every individual estimate as precise. Eligibility, capacity, and customer experience add further constraints. A customer may be highly persuadable but ineligible because of consent rules, recent purchase, contact frequency, or product ownership. A channel may also have limited capacity, making opportunity cost important. Randomized control data is especially valuable because it allows treatment and no-treatment outcomes to be compared under a credible design. When only observational data exists, causal assumptions become stronger and should be stated clearly. Targeting performance should be evaluated using incremental outcomes, not only response rate among contacted customers. A campaign can have a high observed CVR simply because it targets customers who were already likely to buy. A useful workflow separates prediction, causal effect, and decision economics. First estimate relevant outcomes, then estimate how treatment changes them, and finally apply costs, constraints, and policy rules. This framework shifts the question from “Who is most likely to buy?” to “For whom does this action create enough additional value to justify taking it?” That is the difference between predictive ranking and decision-focused targeting.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it.
